title: Large genome models used to design new viruses
gist: Stanford researchers used the Evo 1 and Evo 2 large genome models to generate complete bacteriophage genomes based on ΦX174: 16 of 285 synthesized candidates (5.6 percent) were viable, and AI-suggested variants were vastly more likely to remain functional than random mutation predicts, with nearly a quarter of candidates carrying more than 25 amino acid changes still working. A cocktail of the AI-designed viruses defeated resistant E. coli where a natural phage cocktail failed, while the authors warn the vertebrate-virus exclusion from training data is a voluntary safeguard anyone with enough compute could remove.

themes.theme: Genome models as a separate modality from protein models

insights.claim: AI-for-biology investment has concentrated on protein design because proteins do the catalytic and structural work of cells, but large genome models trained directly on DNA are now a demonstrated second modality that outputs functional coding sequences in bacteria and mimics eukaryotic gene structure.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Protein-design startups are not the whole AI-bio surface area; DNA-native foundation models are a distinct, under-covered capability stack worth mapping separately.
insights.locator: A lot of the AI work in biology

insights.claim: Large genome models are next-token predictors over a four-letter DNA alphabet, which is simpler than natural language, but harder because genomes interleave positions where the next base is critical with long stretches where any base works, forcing the model to infer biological context humans have not yet characterized.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: The signal-to-noise structure of DNA means genome-model quality depends on training corpus breadth more than parameter count — a data-moat argument, not a compute-moat one.
insights.locator: Large language models are essentially trained

insights.claim: Genome models prompted with part of a bacterial gene cluster output DNA encoding proteins with related functions, including working proteins unlike anything previously identified, so the models can generate genuinely novel functional biology rather than recombining known parts.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Novel-function output is the value driver for any IP claim built on genome models; it also raises the dual-use risk premium.
insights.locator: Bacterial genes with related functions tend to cluster

insights.claim: The utility of genome models on complex-cell (eukaryotic) sequence is capped by human ignorance rather than model capability: outputs look like genes and regulatory DNA, but because eukaryotic genes can sit essentially anywhere, there is no way to assay what the hallucinated genes do.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Near-term commercial applications of genome models will cluster in microbial and phage space where validation is cheap, not in human-genome design.
insights.quote: we have no idea what functions these hallucinated genes might perform (if any), so we can’t really test them in any way
insights.locator: But our own lack of knowledge places limits

themes.theme: ΦX174 as the deliberately chosen test harness

insights.claim: The Stanford team tested whole-genome generation on ΦX174, an E. coli bacteriophage with just 11 genes across roughly 5,400 bases where every gene has a known function and the infection cycle is fully characterized, making it the cheapest possible ground truth for scoring AI-designed genomes.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Benchmark choice reveals the field's real frontier: whole-genome synthesis is validated only at ~5kb scale today, which bounds how fast this generalizes.
insights.locator: The model virus they chose as a test case

insights.claim: Prompt engineering was the binding constraint on genome generation: too much of the ΦX174 start sequence made the model regurgitate the original genome verbatim, too little produced unrelated sequence, and only a four-to-nine base prompt window produced useful novel variants.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: The exploitable design window is razor-thin, which means capability here still depends on skilled operators rather than a push-button pipeline.
insights.quote: The researchers eventually found prompts with four to nine bases of the start sequence worked best.

insights.claim: Raw model output was not usable without heavy hand-coded filtering: the team discarded any candidate whose spike protein was under 60 percent identical to the real one, anything below 4,000 or above 6,000 bases, any homopolymer run over 10 bases, and any with anomalous GC/AT frequencies.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Human-authored biological priors still do most of the filtering work — the value in these systems sits in the wrapper and the assay loop, not the base model alone.
insights.locator: For example, ΦX174 uses its own version of a spike protein

themes.theme: Hit rates: how expensive AI-designed genomes actually are

insights.claim: Of 302 computationally screened viral sequences, 285 were chemically synthesized and inserted into bacteria and only 16 inhibited E. coli growth — a 5.6 percent viability rate, with nine working as originally output and seven only after acquiring further mutations in the host.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: A ~6 percent wet-lab hit rate sets the real cost curve for AI genome design: DNA synthesis and screening throughput, not inference, is the bottleneck to fund.
insights.locator: Throwing out those at the computer analysis stage

insights.claim: Viability is steeply conditioned on similarity to the wild-type genome: candidates at 98 percent or greater sequence identity to ΦX174 were viable 46 percent of the time versus 5.6 percent overall, meaning novelty and function trade off almost directly in genome design.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Any claim that a genome model produces 'novel' viable organisms should be stress-tested against sequence-identity distance — the interesting regime is the low-identity tail.
insights.locator: But if you looked only at the outputs that were most similar

insights.claim: ΦX174 is exceptionally fragile to mutation — a single amino-acid-altering base change inactivates it roughly 20 percent of the time, and none of the viable AI-designed viruses carried even one change in the genome-replication origin region.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Fragility of the target explains why the field starts here; more mutation-tolerant genomes would show far higher AI design yields and should be watched as the next benchmark.
insights.quote: ΦX174 doesn’t just fear change; it’s typically murdered by it.
insights.locator: All of that is in keeping with past studies

themes.theme: AI mutation beats random mutation — the core capability claim

insights.claim: Applying the 20-percent-per-change inactivation rate, viruses carrying fewer than 25 amino acid changes should be viable only 2.3 percent of the time and those above 25 changes essentially never — yet nearly a quarter of AI-generated candidates with more than 25 changes were viable, including two with over 50 alterations.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: This is the quantitative proof that genome models encode real epistatic structure, not noise — the single most load-bearing result for valuing the technology.
insights.locator: The researchers did an interesting analysis

insights.claim: Large genome models make coordinated multi-site changes that preserve function far more reliably than random mutation, effectively compressing evolutionary search that natural selection would need many generations to perform.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Search-compression over biological fitness landscapes is the generalizable asset; it transfers to any sequence-design market, from enzymes to therapeutics.
insights.quote: This tells us the AI is far more likely to make changes that leave a viable virus behind than random mutation.
insights.locator: This tells us the AI is far more likely

insights.claim: Individual AI-designed viruses achieved architectural changes that are hard to reach by incremental evolution: one dropped a viral protein entirely and compensated elsewhere in the genome, one added a wholly new gene, and one swapped in a gene from a very distantly related virus.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Gene-level restructuring, not point mutation, is where AI genome design creates capability that natural selection does not readily supply — and where biosecurity concern concentrates.
insights.locator: But, as individuals, the viruses were fairly distinct.

themes.theme: Phage cocktails and the antibiotic-resistance angle

insights.claim: In head-to-head testing a cocktail of natural E. coli bacteriophages failed against resistant hosts while a cocktail of the 16 viable AI-generated viruses rapidly evolved the ability to infect them, apparently by swapping DNA segments among themselves and picking up extra mutations.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: A diverse AI-generated phage library behaves as an adaptive, resistance-breaking system — the first concrete commercial rationale for genome models in anti-infectives.
insights.quote: In their tests, the natural bacteriophage cocktail failed, but the AI-generated group managed to quickly evolve the ability to infect their otherwise resistant hosts.
insights.locator: So the team tested a cocktail of natural bacteriophages

insights.claim: The commercial case for AI-designed phages is discounted by the fact that phage therapy has been under consideration for years without achieving widespread public use despite worsening drug-resistant bacterial infections, implying the barrier is regulatory and clinical rather than technical.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Do not underwrite AI-phage ventures on technical novelty alone; the historical adoption failure of phage therapy is the dominant risk factor.
insights.locator: It’s not clear whether this is a major potential benefit

themes.theme: Dual-use risk and the governance lag

insights.claim: Evo 1 and Evo 2 were deliberately trained without any sequences from viruses that infect complex cells as a precaution, an explicit self-imposed safety carve-out taken before the whole-genome generation experiments.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Training-data exclusion is currently the only real safety control in genome models — a voluntary, unaudited one, which is exactly the kind of gap that invites regulation.
insights.locator: Still, as a precaution while training these models

insights.claim: The safety carve-out is non-durable because anyone with sufficient compute could rerun the same procedure with vertebrate-infecting viruses included in the training data, meaning the barrier to designing a vertebrate-targeting virus is data curation and compute access, not scientific insight.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Compute access and DNA-synthesis order screening become the enforceable chokepoints; expect policy pressure and compliance spend to land on synthesis providers first.
insights.quote: anyone with access to sufficient computing resources could repeat the process with those viruses included
insights.locator: And the authors are very clear that large genome models come with risks

insights.claim: The paper closes with a call for better governance of large genome models and of custom DNA sequence ordering, against a backdrop in which AI regulation has broadly failed to keep pace with the field.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Watch for screening mandates on commercial DNA synthesis vendors — a near-term, concrete regulatory vector distinct from generic AI model rules.
insights.quote: So far, however, regulation of AI has largely failed to keep up with the rapid pace of the field.
insights.locator: The paper ends with a call for better governance
